# YAML

## YAML {.smaller}

We have mappings and keys!

You can think of the "map" as a YAML option. You can think of the "key"
as the value the option takes on.

```         
---
title: "My Document"
---
```

title is the "map" and "My Document" is the key!

Note: When we are working with a simple string, the quotes are optional.
When you are working with things likes numbers that you want to be
treated as text, quotes are necessary.

[Options](https://quarto-tdg.org/yaml.html)

## YAML {.smaller}

What's the difference?

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Example 1**

```{=html}
<pre><code>---
title: "Test Document"
author:
name: Elijah Meyer
affiliation: NC State University
---</code></pre>
```
**Example 2**

```{=html}
<pre><code>---
title: "Test Document"
author:
- name: Elijah Meyer
affiliation: NC State University
---</code></pre>
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Example 3**

```{=html}
<pre><code>---
title: "Test Document"
author:
  - name: Elijah Meyer
    affiliation: NC State University
---</code></pre>
```
:::
:::

## YAML

The `-` is necessary when we have a list item (an item that we could
have multiple of)

```         
author
  └── list item
        ├── name
        └── affiliation
```

**Most** (not all) YAML headings require indentation. This is a good
habit to get into early.

# Objects, Vectors, and Lists 

## R Objects

When we create something in R, such as a number, a word, or a collection of values, R stores it as an object.

```
x <- 10

x + 5
```

## Vectors

A vector is a collection of values.

`c` stands for combine (you can think about this as collection if you would like!)

```
scores <- c(85, 92, 78, 90, 88)
```
```{r}
#| echo: false

scores <- c(85, 92, 78, 90, 88)

str(scores)
```

What type of vector is this? A numeric vector or a character vector?



## Vectors 

We will talk about character vs numeric now, and talk about more types of data types + data coercion later in the semester!

```
cities <- c("Raleigh", "Durham", "Chapel Hill")
```

We can think about characters as **Text** data. These data will have " " around them. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
cities <- c("Raleigh", "Durham", "Chapel Hill")

str(cities)
```

## Indexing{.smaller} 

Sometimes, we want to only look at a subset of our vector. On your own, please run the following code, and take note of what we discover.

```
data <-  c(4,6,7,3,2,5,8)

a) data[2]
b) data[3:6]
c) data[c(1,4,6)]
d) data[-5]
e) data[-c(2,3,5,7)]
```

# Questions 

## Lists{.smaller} 

A list is an object that can contain different kinds of objects! So far, we have discussed character vectors and numeric vectors. 

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

student.temp <- c("Alice", 19, 92, 88, 95)
  
student <- list(
  name = "Alice",
  age = 19,
  scores = c(92, 88, 95)
)
```

## Lists{.smaller}

Let's play around with this list using the `$`. Run the following code and see what we learn. 

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
student$name
student$gpa
student$scores
mean(student$scores)
```


## Lists{.smaller}

So why are lists useful? 

Let's compare our `student` list vs say the data frame `iris` 

```{r}
#| echo: false
head(iris)
```

What's the same? What's different? 

## Lists vs Data Frames
```{r}
#| eval: true
student <- data.frame(
  name = "Alice",
  age = 19,
  major = "Biology",
  score = c(92, 88, 95))

student
```


## Summary 

The components (variables) of a data frame have to be the same length! Lists, they do not. 

A data frame is designed for: Many observations of the same set of variables.

A list is designed for: Putting different kinds of information together.

Or: A list organizes objects; a data frame organizes observations into rows and variables into columns.
